subject: physics
question_text: If the maximum intensity of radiation for a black body is found at 1.45 μm, what is the temperature of radiating body? (Wien’s constant = 2.9 × 10⁻³ mK)

verification.note: Asked in TS Inter I-Year Physics Paper-I, March 2019 (Q7) — Section A, 2 marks. The 1 + 1 mark split is INVENTED and is a CLAIM until a Telangana IPE teacher confirms it; the question itself is sourced from that paper. Arithmetic hand-checked: λₘ = 1.45 μm = 1.45 × 10⁻⁶ m; T = b / λₘ = 2.9 × 10⁻³ / 1.45 × 10⁻⁶; 2.9 ÷ 1.45 = 2 and 10⁻³ ÷ 10⁻⁶ = 10³, so T = 2 × 10³ K = 2000 K.

recall_prompt: Say the steps you would write for this answer, in order. You can speak in English, in Telugu, or in both.

steps.margin_note: First mark. The unit conversion is written here, never assumed.
steps.why: Wien’s law connects the wavelength of maximum intensity to the absolute temperature. The constant is quoted in metre kelvin, so the wavelength has to be in metres before the division.
common_mistakes: Dividing by 1.45 without converting micrometres to metres, which makes the answer 10⁶ times too small.

recall.must_convey: That λₘT = b and that 1.45 μm must be written as 1.45 × 10⁻⁶ m.

steps.memory_tip: 1 μm = 10⁻⁶ m. The constant is in metre kelvin, so the wavelength must be in metres.

steps.margin_note: Second mark. The number 2000 with the unit K is what is checked.
steps.why: Dividing 2.9 by 1.45 gives 2, and 10⁻³ divided by 10⁻⁶ gives 10³, so the temperature is 2 × 10³ K.
common_mistakes: Leaving the answer as 2 × 10³ with no unit. The unit K is part of the mark.

insider_note: Two marks: one for λₘT = b with the metre conversion, one for the value 2000 K. The unit K is part of the second mark.
